entries.test: The four named companies' cumulative AI capital expenditures through the end of 2027 and their disclosed AI revenue and operating results would test the claim.

entries.test: Meta's published GEM performance metrics and their definitions across the cited quarters would show whether its reporting is inconsistent.

entries.test: The named companies' cumulative AI spending and disclosed AI revenues and products as of publication would test the factual assertions.

entries.test: OpenAI's reported 2026 loss and its shares of Microsoft's AI revenue and GPU capacity at publication would settle the numerical claims.

entries.test: Customer revenue concentration and the labs' financial statements would show the extent of Microsoft's and Amazon's dependence on OpenAI and Anthropic.
entries.note: The Google extension is explicitly tentative; the Microsoft and Amazon dependency assertion is firm.

entries.test: Microsoft's Q3 FY2025 AI run rate and OpenAI's Azure inference spending for that quarter would establish the stated ratio under the author's annualization assumption.
entries.note: The source conditions the comparison on a run rate being consistent throughout the quarter. The normalization drops that assumption.

entries.test: Published Microsoft revenue records or authenticated billing documents for Q2 FY2025 would settle the infrastructure, Copilot and OpenAI spending amounts.
entries.note: The figures conflict with another Q2 inference figure in the post; that affects accuracy, not checkability.

entries.test: OpenAI's Azure inference billing near the end of 2025, annualized on the stated basis, would test the $18.5 billion estimate.
entries.note: The normalization preserves the estimate but omits its explicit exclusion of Sora 2 and Codex.

entries.test: Microsoft's AI revenue by customer and its infrastructure allocation at publication would establish OpenAI's revenue and capacity shares.
entries.note: The proposition drops 'I estimate' and narrows 'its infrastructure' to AI infrastructure.
The payment ceiling is expressly qualified by 'likely'.

entries.test: Microsoft's GPU allocation records or public customer-capacity disclosures would establish whether OpenAI occupied at least 80% at publication.
entries.note: The normalization omits the caveat that Anthropic might now occupy some of that capacity. A numerical estimate remains testable.

entries.test: Fairwater capacity agreements and Microsoft or OpenAI disclosures would establish whether all its data centers were reserved for OpenAI.
entries.note: This concerns reservations, not whether construction was complete.

entries.test: Microsoft's cumulative capital expenditures and quarterly AI revenue excluding OpenAI would settle both amounts.
Anthropic's AWS spending run rate and Amazon's AI revenue run rate at publication would test the $12 billion and 80% estimates.
entries.note: The source adopts a numerical assumption; the normalization recasts it as 'likely'. It describes an estimated current amount, not future spending.

entries.test: Amazon's total AI capacity and the capacity allocated to Anthropic at publication would establish whether Anthropic's share exceeded 75%.
entries.note: The normalization drops the explicitly assumed character of the estimate. 'Confident' does not trigger the probability-language exclusion.

entries.test: Alphabet's reported Google Cloud revenues for Q3 2025, Q4 2025 and Q1 2026 would settle the quarterly growth comparison and percentages.
entries.note: The quoted percentages can be checked independently of the direction of the comparison.
The central assertion attributes a private purpose to Google's reporting choices.
He presents this explanation as something that 'might' be a reason.

entries.test: The Dwarkesh interview transcript and publicly available evidence cited for Anthropic's inference profitability would show whether the claims rest solely on non-Anthropic illustrative figures.
entries.note: 'Unsupported' softens the source's stronger accusation that people are making the claim up.
The source says the timing 'suggests' causation; the proposition asserts causation outright.

entries.test: The Google, Broadcom and Anthropic purchase, installation and rental agreements would show whether Anthropic both buys the TPUs and pays Google to rent them back.

entries.note: Whether funded purchases count as 'real demand' has no agreed factual threshold.
The claim combines a factual financing assertion with an explicit judgment that the relationships should be illegal.
The passage supplies no shared criterion for 'real, meaningful' demand or for what investment behavior establishes its absence.

entries.test: The named hyperscalers' AI customer revenue shares and the labs' losses, cash flows and operating economics would test the asserted concentration and dependence on funding.
entries.note: Read 'hyperscaler' here as the three named companies. The categorical profitability assertion can be challenged with a demonstrably viable business model.
The selected proposition asserts a private intention to deceive.

entries.test: Google's total compute capacity and Anthropic's allocated capacity at publication would test the estimate of at least half of 2.95 GW.
entries.note: The proposition omits 'I estimate'.

entries.test: The three companies' capital expenditure allocations, capacity utilization by customer and the labs' cash flows would test the allocation and funding claims.
entries.note: The source says the capacity is 'mostly used' by the labs; the normalization weakens that to merely 'used'.
'May kill Oracle' states a possibility, not a firm prediction.

entries.test: Industry AI revenue totals and compute demand attributed to OpenAI and Anthropic at publication would test their combined 70% share.
entries.note: The normalization omits the explicit estimate qualifier. Defining the denominator is necessary but does not make a numerical market-share claim uncheckable.

entries.test: The labs' annual losses, financing cash flows and shares of AI revenue and compute spending would test the asserted industry dependence on fundraising.
Public financial evidence showing a viable route to profitability or a sustainable alternative to the asserted funding dependence would test the proposition.
entries.note: 'I have yet to see any proof' does not assert that no proof exists anywhere.

entries.test: Anthropic's investor projections and contemporaneous financial obligations would show whether an $11 billion annual burn projection materially understated its expected cash needs.
entries.note: The normalization removes 'I think'. This concerns the accuracy of a present investor representation, not just eventual annual burn.

entries.test: Anthropic's financing disclosures, compute contracts and advance-payment cash flows would show whether fundraising was required to pay for unbuilt capacity.
entries.note: The source qualifies this as an argument and says Anthropic is 'having to' raise the money; the normalization omits both.

entries.test: Anthropic's reported or authenticated full-year 2025 revenue would settle whether the $4.5 billion reports were false.
entries.note: The source alleges knowing falsehood by sources and qualifies that with 'I think'; the normalization changes this to factual inaccuracy alone.

entries.test: Anthropic's capacity disclosures, customer intake and published service uptime records around publication would test whether it added customers while struggling to exceed 99% availability.
entries.note: 'Greedily' is evaluative, but the customer and uptime assertions are factual.
This is an ethical recommendation.
The source offers a personal causal explanation, which the normalization states directly. 'Something peculiar' identifies no specific accounting practice to test.
The proposition turns a mocking description qualified by 'does not appear' into a categorical statement about strategy.
The selected description is invective rather than an operational claim about financial distress.

entries.test: Whether the named companies cease operating or fail as businesses as a result of an AI bubble collapse would test the prediction.
entries.note: The post subsequently states the same prediction firmly: 'these companies will not die'.

entries.test: Deployment, retirement and commercial usefulness of the NVIDIA GPUs bought in the cited period would show whether they were almost entirely obsolete by 2030.
entries.note: 'Obsolete' has a plain reading of no longer practically competitive or useful, even without a numerical performance cutoff.

entries.test: The companies' reported growth and depreciation expenses would show how much rising depreciation offsets their operating gains.
entries.note: The source refers to depreciation generally; the normalization restricts it to GPUs.

entries.test: The named companies' segment results and quantified sources of incremental revenue would show whether AI contributes little or nothing to their current growth.

entries.note: Reporting formats are public, but the central allegation is a private intent to obscure revenue.

entries.test: Authenticated Microsoft revenue schedules and its public financial disclosures would show whether itemized AI revenues exist internally and are withheld externally.
entries.note: The concrete claim concerns existing records and disclosure choices, without specifying a hidden motive.
This asks the media to take an action.
This is explicitly a counterfactual scenario. The normalization also drops the requirement that other services continue growing.

entries.test: The companies' disclosed backlog by customer and the labs' available cash and financing would test the 50% concentration and current payment capacity.
entries.note: The normalization substitutes backlog for the source's broader 'upcoming revenues' and removes its specific, inconsistent company list. The ultimate funding-source component is prospective.

entries.test: AI service revenues, compute purchases and contracted demand excluding OpenAI and Anthropic would show their scale relative to the cited capital investment.
entries.note: The central assertion is that demand outside the two labs is very small; the investment-justification language adds judgment.
'Their compute' has an ambiguous denominator that the normalization resolves without qualification. The purpose of artificially inflating revenue is an attributed private motive.
This sweeping denunciation supplies no distinct threshold for the allegedly false demand story.

entries.test: Amazon's and Microsoft's annualized AI revenues divided by their cumulative capital expenditures would test the claimed roughly 6% ratios.
entries.note: The normalization restricts the denominator to AI capex; the selected sentence says capital expenditures.

entries.note: The affordability assertion concerns current resources, not a guaranteed future default.

entries.note: 'Manipulate' is more specific and accusatory than 'doing weird things'. The categorical profitability assertion is still testable.

entries.test: Public AI-specific profit disclosures from the companies discussed in the post would establish whether any can show a profit from AI.

The proposition adds investors as the specific audience and omits the asserted sources of non-AI growth. An exclusive explanation of collective tolerance attributes private motivations.

Expressing surprise at an outcome assigns it a low likelihood rather than ruling it out.
Neither 'killing the product as they know it' nor invalidating every growth story identifies an agreed outcome.

entries.test: AI revenue by customer and contractual payment dependencies would establish which hyperscalers rely on Anthropic, OpenAI or both.
entries.note: The normalization erases the distinct company-to-lab dependencies stated in the source.
The source predicts becoming tired of the arrangement, a private attitude. 'Pull back' adds an observable action not specified in this sentence.
'Reckon with' specifies neither an action nor an outcome most readers would test alike.
The metaphors do not identify what event counts as the frenzy stopping or somebody blinking.

entries.test: GPU shipment volumes, installation throughput and inventory reports at publication would test the six-month deployment ratio and warehouse accumulation.
Comparable estimates of capital and market value involved in the AI boom and historical speculative bubbles would test the claim that it is the largest.

Neither deterioration nor increased narrative attachment and agitation has a shared test in this passage.
